summary.one_line: A real, fast-growing maker of LAN, fibre and specialty cables with about 22% of India's networking-cable market, but growth has come with negative operating cash flow, a 7x rise in debt, heavy customer concentration and a live lawsuit over its own name. 42% of the issue is a promoter exit. Worth tracking, not buying at the IPO.
bull_points: Revenue from operations grew from Rs 6,577.67 mn in FY24 to Rs 11,716.54 mn in FY26, and Q1 FY27 alone brought in Rs 4,891.56 mn at an 11.22% EBITDA margin (S1).
Market position is real: a claimed ~22% share of India's networking-cables market in FY25, up from ~16% in FY22, and it supplies two of India's top three telecom companies (S3).
Customers stay: 98.78% of FY25 revenue from its top 50 customers came from repeat customers, and it has worked with its top 10 customers for more than eight years on average (S3).
Most of the fresh money (Rs 1,555 mn of Rs 3,200 mn) goes to repaying debt, which should cut the Rs 2,584.57 mn of borrowings held at June 2026 by about 60% (S1)(S7).
bear_points: Operating cash flow was negative in FY25 (-Rs 97.85 mn), FY26 (-Rs 266.44 mn) and Q1 FY27 (-Rs 117.64 mn), even though the company reported more than Rs 1,400 mn of profit over those periods (S1).
Total borrowings rose from Rs 367.31 mn (FY24) to Rs 2,584.57 mn (June 2026), and net working capital days went from 14 to 46-48 (S1).
The top 10 customers made up 84.00% of Q1 FY27 revenue, and the single largest customer made up 38.54% (S1).

Orient Electric has sued in the Delhi High Court to stop the company using the ORIENT name, asking for an injunction and Rs 2 crore in damages. Settlement talks are under way and the next hearing is on 2 December 2026 (S8).
FY26 profit after tax barely moved (Rs 538.13 mn vs Rs 533.21 mn) despite 42% revenue growth, and the PAT margin fell to 4.55% (S1).
watch_points: Whether the Orient Electric name/trademark dispute is settled, and on what terms, before or at the 2 December 2026 hearing (S8).
Whether operating cash flow turns positive after listing once debt is repaid, and whether working-capital days come back down from 46-48 (S1).
When the capex is actually spent: the RHP schedule puts most of it in FY28 and FY29, no purchase orders have been placed yet, and quotations are valid for six months (S7).
Any refresh of the lapsed CRISIL rating, which was last CRISIL B/Stable (Issuer not cooperating) (S1).

reasoning: Operating cash flow does not yet back up the reported profits. Over FY25, FY26 and Q1 FY27 the company booked about Rs 1,404 mn of PAT but used about Rs 482 mn in operations, and borrowings rose about 7x to Rs 2,584.57 mn (S1). Until one or two listed quarters show profits turning into cash, the growth story is being paid for with debt.

The use of the money is defensible but defensive. Roughly half the fresh issue (Rs 1,555 mn) repays debt, only Rs 915 mn funds capex spread over FY27-FY29 with no orders placed, and a further Rs 2,320 mn (42% of the issue) is an OFS paying out promoters whose average acquisition cost is Rs 0.00-0.01 per share (S1)(S7).

There is some moat, but it is narrow. Customer qualification audits taking about six months, certifications (UL, ETL, CPR, BIS, RDSO, TSEC) and a claimed ~22% networking-cable share are real barriers (S3). But the peers named in its own prospectus (Polycab, KEI, Finolex, Havells, RR Kabel, Sterlite, Birla Cable) are far larger, and customer concentration of 84% in the top 10 limits its pricing power (S1)(S3).

The company's own name is under legal attack. Orient Electric's suit asks for an injunction against the ORIENT marks and corporate name, and it is still pending with settlement talks under way (S8). The worst outcome is a forced rebrand of a B2B supplier, which is manageable but not priced into any disclosure we saw.

Governance is acceptable but not clean. RPTs are small and routine (rent to a promoter company, promoter loans now repaid), but there are repeated CARO mismatches between stock statements given to banks and the books, late CSR and TDS deposits, a lapsed CRISIL B rating after the company stopped cooperating, and a promoter-group relative listed as a wilful defaulter (S3). Each is minor; together they justify waiting for a listed track record.

subsections.title: What it makes and how revenue is earned

blocks.text: Orient Cables was incorporated in September 2005 and started making LAN cables at Bhiwadi, Rajasthan in 2006. It describes itself as a manufacturer focused on networking cables and passive networking equipment, selling into broadband, telecom, data centres, renewables, smart building automation/security, system integration, FMEG and automotive (S1)(S3). It is a pure B2B supplier, and nearly everything it sells is made to customer specifications. Customers send technical specs, and Orient designs, samples, gets approval, runs a prototype order and then scales up (S3).

blocks.caption: Revenue by product segment (Rs mn, % of revenue from operations) - restated
rows: Networking Cables and Solutions (CAT5e/6/6A LAN, patch cords, CCTV/coax)
Specialty Power, Optical Fibre Cables and Solutions
Wire/cable harness, EV charging gun cable assembly

blocks.text: The mix is changing quickly. Specialty power and optical fibre rose from 11.89% of revenue in FY25 to 31.23% in Q1 FY27 (S1). The fibre range covers Unitube and Multitube cables of up to 288 fibres, fibre patch cords, low-tension power cables and terminated power assemblies used in telecom infrastructure (S3). New lines such as harnesses, EV charging guns, keystone jacks, power strips, solar junction boxes and tethered-drone cable systems together still bring in less than 1% of revenue (S1)(S3).

blocks.caption: Revenue by end-user industry, FY25 (Rs mn) - DRHP

blocks.text: Broadband is the demand driver behind 57% of revenue. Data centres are often quoted in IPO marketing but made up only 2.77% of FY25 revenue, and that share fell from 5.52% in FY24 (S3).

The company names three customer types: large customers (telecom service providers, telecom equipment makers, power utilities), OEMs and resellers (S1). It does not name its top 10 customers, citing missing consents and commercial sensitivity (S1). The DRHP describes a case study of one top-10 customer, a global maker of networking, hardware and telecom equipment. That relationship started with LAN cables and patch cords in India in 2012, added CCTV (2017), OFC (2019) and UAE supply (2021), and in 2024 moved on to keystone jacks (S3).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration (% of revenue from operations)

blocks.text: Concentration has risen, not fallen, as the company has grown. The top 10 went from 71.76% of revenue in FY24 to 84.00% in Q1 FY27, and the largest customer alone contributed Rs 1,885.39 mn in that quarter (S1). Purchase orders are the main contracting tool, and some of them can be terminated without cause (S3). Exports are shrinking as a share of sales: from 13.15% of revenue in FY24 to 9.26% in FY26 and 7.00% in Q1 FY27, and most of it goes to the UAE and Qatar (S1).
In Q1 FY27 a single unnamed customer accounted for 38.54% of revenue (S1). The loss or repricing of that one account would change the whole investment case, and investors cannot identify it.

The company runs two manufacturing units at Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, near the Garhi Harsaru and Rewari inland container depots. The RHP also lists a manufacturing facility in Bengaluru for networking, specialty power and fibre cables (S1)(S3). Unit I (in operation since 2006) makes LAN cables, power cables and keystone jacks. Unit II (fibre added in 2018) makes LAN, power and fibre cables, patch cords, power strips and harnesses, and houses an e-beam irradiation facility (S3). Both plants sit on 99-year leases from RIICO (S3).

Sources: FY23-FY25 from the DRHP (S3); June 2026 capacity from the RHP summaries (S6)(S14); FY26 utilisation of 69.85% as reported by Trade Brains from the RHP (S12). On an annualised basis FY25 capacity was 794,976 km, with Unit II's capacity lifted from 332,941 km to 568,256 km during that year (S3). With utilisation already below 70% in FY26, adding another 359,520 km should be read as a bet on future demand, not a fix for a current bottleneck (S7)(S12).

Main raw materials are copper, PVC/HDPE/LDPE compounds and masterbatches. The company makes some inputs in-house: PVC compound (a 500 MT/month line), drawn copper, and FRP rods and impregnated fibreglass yarn for fibre cables (S3). Aside from annual copper contracts and 3-6 month fibre supply agreements, it buys on short-term purchase orders and keeps 20-25 days of raw material and work-in-progress (S3). Supplier concentration is high: the top 10 suppliers provided 77.93% of raw materials in FY25 and 74.91% in Q1 FY27 (S1)(S3). Copper is priced off the LME, and the company has no commodity hedging policy (S3).

The company had 447 permanent employees and 1,050 contract workers as of March 2025 (S3). It relies on contract labour, and in FY21-FY25 it ran Unit II above the capacity allowed by its pollution consent until it paid a Rs 0.33 mn penalty and got a revised consent (S3).

All industry figures come from a report by 1Lattice that the company commissioned and paid for, so they should be treated as a sales document, not an independent forecast (S3). According to that report, India's networking-cables market grew from about Rs 20.6 bn in FY22 to about Rs 35.9 bn in FY26. The Indian fibre-optic cable market is projected to grow from about Rs 105.0 bn in FY26 to Rs 233.1 bn by FY31, a CAGR of about 17.3% (S1). The DRHP version put the broader Indian broadband-cables market at Rs 118.4 bn in FY25, projected to reach Rs 257.2 bn by FY30 (16.8% CAGR) (S3).

The demand case rests on India's low fixed-broadband penetration (under 5% in CY2023, per the report), fibre-to-the-home rollouts, BharatNet, 5G backhaul and data-centre build-outs (S3). These are real long-term trends, but they tie Orient's volumes to telecom and broadband capex cycles run by a small number of large buyers. That is the same concentration seen in its customer list (S1).

subsections.title: Competitors and whether there is a moat

blocks.text: The company's own risk factors name its competitors: RR Kabel, Polycab, Finolex Cables, Havells, KEI Industries, Paramount Communications, Birla Cable and Sterlite Technologies, with Belden India also in the peer set (S3). Most of these are much larger, diversified wire-and-cable companies that can price aggressively or bundle products. Sterlite and Birla Cable compete directly in optical fibre (S3).

items: Market share claim: one of India's top five networking-cable makers, with about 22% share in FY25, up from about 16% in FY22 (S3). The RHP-era summaries describe it as about 22.9% share among the top four players (S6). This is the strongest point in its favour, although it comes from the paid report.

Qualification barrier: customers audit plants and test samples abroad before placing orders, a process the report says takes about six months (S3). This is a real switching cost for incumbents like Orient and a hurdle for new small entrants, but it does not stop Polycab or KEI.

Certifications: UL (CM/CMR), ETL, CPR for Europe, BIS 14493 for LAN cables (the company says BIS invited it to help draft the standard), TSEC for BSNL fibre and RDSO for railways (S3). These are needed to compete; large peers hold them too.

'First' claims: first Indian company to get BIS certification for symmetrical pair/quad cables, and an early mover in organised keystone-jack manufacturing (S3). These are narrow niches, not a durable moat.
Cost position: the report says its products are cost-competitive against China (S3). This is an import-substitution angle, but no protective duty or regulatory barrier is disclosed.

blocks.text: Verdict on moat: there is some advantage from scale in a niche, long customer relationships and certifications, but nothing structural like a patent, licence or regulatory exclusivity. Its main customers are large telecom and networking buyers with strong bargaining power, and FY26's falling margins (EBITDA 8.23% vs 10.17%) show how little pricing power it has (S1).

Figures are from the RHP's restated financials (S1). FY23 revenue was Rs 5,436.78 mn and PAT Rs 259.59 mn, per the DRHP (S3). YoY growth for FY24 and FY25 is from the DRHP (S3), and FY26 growth is calculated from S1. The DRHP gave FY25 PAT as Rs 532.91 mn, slightly different from the RHP's Rs 533.21 mn (S3)(S1).

The trend is mixed. Revenue has more than doubled since FY23, but FY26 added Rs 3,467 mn of revenue and only about Rs 5 mn of extra PAT, as EBITDA margin dropped nearly two points and finance costs rose with debt (S1). Q1 FY27 looks much stronger (Rs 4,891.56 mn revenue in a quarter, 11.22% EBITDA margin). But that quarter was driven by the specialty power/fibre segment and a 38.54% single-customer share (S1). A lumpy quarter just before an IPO should not be annualised.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, cash flow and working capital

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow (Rs mn)

blocks.text: This is the weakest part of the story. Since FY24, operating cash flow has turned negative three periods in a row, and borrowings have been used to pay for both working capital and capex. Financing inflows were Rs 1,016.61 mn in FY26 alone (S1). Independent reviewers make the same point, flagging two consecutive years of negative operating cash flow alongside a rising debt/equity ratio (S13). Working-capital days have more than tripled from 14 to 46-48 (S1). The DRHP shows the cause in FY25: inventory rose from Rs 403.53 mn to Rs 757.54 mn and receivables from Rs 1,364.09 mn to Rs 1,621.68 mn, and the company says payment terms run up to 120 days (S3).

Cash-flow and profit mismatch: cumulative PAT for FY25 to Q1 FY27 was about Rs 1,404 mn, against about Rs 482 mn of cumulative operating cash outflow (S1). Reported profit is not yet turning into cash. The company lists this as a top-10 risk factor itself (S1).

Other balance-sheet points: at March 2025 the company held Rs 74.86 mn of unsecured debt instruments and had Rs 1,020.14 mn of letters of credit outstanding as contingent liabilities (S3). Capex jumped to Rs 807.31 mn in FY25 (9.79% of revenue) from Rs 168.16 mn in FY24 (S3), while gross fixed-asset turnover fell from 8.44x to 5.81x by FY26 (S1).

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: Partly. Revenue momentum and share gains are real and backed by audited, restated numbers (S1)(S3). But returns are falling (ROE 37.26% to 25.84%, ROCE 41.13% to 23.82% between FY24 and FY26), margins have not scaled with revenue, and growth has been funded by the balance sheet, not by cash from operations (S1). Much of the IPO's fresh money is effectively being used to undo that leverage (S1).

items: Supports the story: revenue CAGR of 33.46% over FY24-FY26 and a rising share of higher-value specialty power/fibre products (S1).
Undercuts it: FY26 PAT was flat, operating cash flow negative, net debt/equity rose from 0.23x to 0.95x, and utilisation was under 70% in FY26 (S1)(S12).
Unresolved: whether Q1 FY27's 11.22% margin can be repeated, or depends on one customer and one product mix (S1).

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

subsections.title: Structure: fresh issue vs offer for sale

blocks.text: Amounts are from the RHP abridged prospectus (S1), which was filed with the RoC on 21 September 2026 (S2). Share counts are from Chittorgarh at the Rs 272 upper band (S6)(S15)(S19). The DRHP was filed on 10 July 2025, and an addendum followed in November 2025 (S4)(S5). The price band is Rs 258-272, the lot is 55 shares (Rs 14,960 at the top of the band), and the allocation is at most 50% to QIBs, at least 35% to retail and at least 15% to NIIs (S6)(S16). The issue runs from 25 to 29 September 2026, with allotment on 30 September and a tentative BSE/NSE listing on 5 October 2026 (S6). IIFL Capital and JM Financial are the book-running lead managers and KFin is the registrar (S1).

42% of the issue (Rs 232 cr of Rs 552 cr) is an OFS and raises nothing for the company (S1). The selling promoters' weighted average acquisition cost is Rs 0.00-0.01 per share, because their holdings largely came from a 9:1 bonus issue in January 2025 (S1)(S3). The OFS was cut from Rs 380 cr in the DRHP to Rs 232 cr in the RHP (S18)(S1). Promoter holding falls from 100% to about 82.17% after the issue (S6).

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds (Rs mn)
rows: Capex: machinery, equipment and civil works at manufacturing facilities
Balance (capped at 25% of gross fresh issue)

blocks.text: Amounts are from the RHP abridged prospectus (S1). The capex deployment schedule and the timing of debt repayment are as reported by Multibagg from the RHP (S7). The DRHP had planned to spend the capex over FY26-FY28 and repay debt in FY26 (S3), so the schedule has moved back by about a year. As of 30 June 2026, borrowings of Rs 2,584.6 mn included Rs 2,404.3 mn of secured fund-based facilities (S7). If the full Rs 1,555 mn is used as planned, gross debt at June 2026 levels would fall by about 60%, but the ongoing need for working capital will pull it back up unless cash conversion improves (S1).

The capex is meant to add 359,520 km of cable capacity (from 895,776 km to 1,255,296 km, +40.1%) and 1.22 crore pieces of allied products a year at Unit II (S7). Main items include six composite extrusion lines (Rs 17.21 cr), two electron-beam accelerators (Rs 17.10 cr), 48 high-speed bunching machines (Rs 13.03 cr), e-beam reactor civil works (Rs 6.90 cr) and a CAT-8 LAN testing system (Rs 3.45 cr) (S7). Vendor quotes add up to Rs 99.79 cr against the Rs 91.50 cr allocated, and the gap is to be met from internal accruals (S7). In the DRHP, most of the quoted machinery came from Chinese vendors such as First Dragon (CN) and CGN Dasheng (S3).

No purchase orders or definitive supplier agreements had been signed by the prospectus date, and the quotations are valid for six months (S7). The capex amount has not been appraised by any bank or financial institution (S3).

The promoters are Vipul Nagpal (54, Chairman and MD, B.Com (Hons) from SRCC and MBA from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, with the company since its incorporation in 2005), his wife Garima Nagpal (48, Whole-time Director, oversees people and talent), their son Vardaan Nagpal (24, Whole-time Director since March 2025, King's College London, FIDE International Master, responsible for strategic initiatives and M&A), and two family trusts (S1). Before the IPO the promoters own 100% of the company: the two trusts hold 35.00% each, Vipul 24.23%, Garima 5.67% and Vardaan 0.10% (S1).

The board has three independent directors: Anil Gupta, Rohit Himatsingka and Manu Narang Wadhwa (S1). The RHP names Rahul Sharma as CFO (S1). The DRHP had named Rakesh Khurmi as CFO, described as having 26 years in finance at telecom and broadband companies (S3). That means the CFO changed between the DRHP and the RHP, a year before listing. Farogh Alam, EVP Operations, has 19 years in cables (S3). Vardaan Nagpal's senior role and M&A mandate rest on about six years' association with the company and no disclosed outside operating experience (S1).

Outside ventures: the promoter group includes Bedrock Estates, Daulat Ispat, the Elektron lighting entities, Imperial Motors, Orient Networks and Paragon Cable India (being struck off) (S3). Vipul Nagpal left Mangalam Markfinvest (2022) and Orient International (March 2025), both of which ceased operations (S3). Orient Networks' charter allows it to make cables, but it is dormant and signed a non-compete with the company in June 2025 (S3).

blocks.caption: Key RPTs (Rs mn) - DRHP
rows: Orient Networks Pvt Ltd (99% Vipul Nagpal)

blocks.text: Data is from the DRHP offer-document summary (S3). Two items stand out. First, in FY25 the company bought Rs 86.75 mn of capex from Orient International, a promoter-linked firm that then closed on 31 March 2025 (S3). The DRHP does not disclose what was bought. Second, promoters and their parents lent money to the company for several years, with Rs 138.82 mn of loans payable at FY23. All of it had been repaid by FY25 (S3). Both the registered office (owned by Vipul Nagpal, Rs 0.01 mn a month) and the corporate office (Orient Networks, Rs 0.40 mn a month) are rented from promoters (S3).

Overall, the RPTs are small (none above about 1% of revenue in any year) and mostly routine: office rent, promoter loans now repaid, and remuneration (S3). The one-off Rs 86.75 mn capex purchase from a promoter firm that has since closed is the only item worth asking about. Customers and suppliers are not related parties, and the DRHP says promoters have no interest in the capex vendors (S3).

items: Credit rating: CRISIL downgraded the company from BB+ to B/Stable, and the rating has been 'Issuer not cooperating' since January 2023. The company says it was not required to have a rating, so it stopped sharing information. It has had no rating since FY25 (S1)(S3).

CARO observations: in FY24 and FY25 the quarterly stock and receivables statements given to banks did not match the books. The largest gap was Rs 137.39 mn of receivables in March 2024, caused by revenue reversals under Ind AS 115 (S3).

Late statutory deposits: CSR money for FY23 and FY24 was moved to the special account after the deadline, and a suo-moto compounding application was filed in June 2025. Small TDS amounts were also paid late (S3).
Environmental: Unit II ran above its consent-to-operate capacity from April 2021 until a penalty of Rs 0.33 mn was paid and a revised consent issued (S3).

Wilful defaulter: Radhika Julka, Vipul Nagpal's sister and a promoter-group member, appears on a wilful-defaulter list over loans to Julka Sons from IDBI Bank. The company says the loan has been repaid but the bank's NOC is still awaited. She has no role in the company (S1)(S3).

Litigation (RHP): against the company, 5 tax cases, 1 statutory/regulatory proceeding and 2 material civil cases totalling Rs 20.40 mn. Vipul Nagpal is the complainant in a Rs 228 mn cheque-bounce case against Shakthi Sona Solar Electric (filed 2017), and the DRHP also disclosed an NCLT claim against ATS Infrastructure related to a property buy-back scheme (S1)(S3).

blocks.text: None of these points alone is a deal-breaker, and the auditor has not qualified the accounts (S1). But taken together, repeated bank-statement mismatches, deadlines missed until shortly before the IPO, and a rating left to lapse suggest a family-run company whose reporting controls are still catching up with its size. The company says the relevant SOPs have now been tightened (S3).

subsections.title: The risks that could change the decision

items: 1. Brand/name litigation. Orient Electric has asked the MCA Regional Director to change the company's name (August 2025) and filed a Delhi High Court suit (November 2025) seeking an injunction on ORIENT marks, trade names and domains, plus Rs 2 crore in damages. Orient Cables has filed a counter-suit. Settlement talks are under way and the next hearing is on 2 December 2026 (S8). The RHP moved this to the top of its risk list (S1).

2. Customer concentration. The top 10 customers made up 84.00% of revenue and the largest 38.54% in Q1 FY27. Customers are unnamed and buy on purchase orders, some of which can be terminated (S1)(S3).
3. Cash flow and leverage. Operating cash flow was negative in FY25, FY26 and Q1 FY27, borrowings rose to Rs 2,584.57 mn, and working-capital days reached 46-48 (S1).

4. Raw-material and supplier concentration. The top 10 suppliers provided 74.91% of inputs in Q1 FY27. Copper and PVC prices move with the LME and crude, the company has no hedging policy, and contracts are mostly short-term (S1)(S3).

5. Execution on capex and underused capacity. FY26 utilisation was about 69.85%, but the company is adding 40% more cable capacity. Orders have not been placed, deployment is backloaded to FY28-FY29 and e-beam is a new technology for the company (S7)(S12).
6. Single-location concentration. Both main plants are in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, and a local disruption would hit most of its output (S1).
7. Governance and reporting controls. The CRISIL rating has lapsed, CARO mismatches recur, a promoter-group relative is listed as a wilful defaulter, and statutory deposits were late (S1)(S3).

blocks.text: The name dispute is unusual among IPO risks because the company is fighting over its own brand in court while listing under that brand. An adverse injunction would force a rebrand of the company and possibly its products (S8).

subsections.title: Risks that are mostly boilerplate here

blocks.text: The foreign-exchange risk is small: net FX gains were Rs 36.00 mn in FY25 (0.44% of revenue), and exports have fallen to 7% of revenue (S1)(S3). Product-quality risk is disclosed, but there have been no recalls or warranty claims in FY23-FY25 and only one customer return, in April 2024 (S3). Contract-labour risk is general to the sector (S3).

Technology substitution is a mild long-term risk. Copper LAN cabling faces gradual replacement by fibre and wireless at the edge. The company is hedging by growing its fibre business, which rose to 31% of revenue in Q1 FY27 when combined with specialty power (S1).
The commissioned industry report is a risk in itself: 1Lattice was paid by the company for the IPO, and every market-share and market-size claim in the prospectus depends on it (S3).

We found no investor call, earnings guidance or interview with management giving revenue, margin or volume targets. News coverage around the price-band announcement restates the prospectus, and the only management statement quoted is the standard line that listing will improve visibility and brand image (S16)(S17). The only forward-looking material is the prospectus's strategy section, which is qualitative (S3).

items: Build on networking-cable and fibre positions to benefit from broadband, FTTH and data-centre demand (S1)(S3).

Diversify into e-beam irradiated cables (for solar, railways, defence), solar junction boxes, passive networking components (faceplates, gang boxes, patch panels, racks), harnesses, power cords, tethered-drone systems and EV charging guns through subsidiary OCL Greentech, incorporated May 2025 (S3).
Expand exports into Europe, Australia and the US by following existing multinational customers, as it did in the UAE (S3).

Add capacity in phases (+359,520 km cable, +1.22 crore pieces) and deepen backward integration in copper drawing and polymer compounding (S3)(S7). A proposed Unit III at Bhiwadi is on an 11-month lease, and land at Choupanki, Rajasthan was bought in May 2025 (S3).

blocks.text: The company says it has trial or early orders for tethered-drone systems and power cords, and received orders from two customers for power strips (S3). The RHP's FY26 and Q1 FY27 numbers show these new lines still make up less than 1% of revenue (S1).

In the near term the business will be driven by broadband and telecom capex from a few large customers, and by the move towards fibre and specialty power, which went from 11.89% to 31.23% of revenue in five quarters (S1). The capex being funded mainly adds capacity to a business that used about 70% of its capacity in FY26 (S12). That makes the payoff depend on winning more volume, not on removing a bottleneck.

Management has not given concrete guidance. Any growth figure seen in IPO marketing either comes from the paid 1Lattice market forecasts or projects past growth forward, and neither is a company commitment (S3).

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: Anchor book (24 September 2026): the company raised about Rs 165.6 crore by allotting 60.88 lakh shares at Rs 272, the top of the band (S9). IPO Central reported 20 anchor investors, including eight domestic mutual funds and two life insurers, with domestic MFs taking more than two-thirds (S20). Named anchors include Nippon Life India, ICICI Prudential AMC, Aditya Birla Sun Life AMC, Goldman Sachs and Border to Coast Pensions Partnership (S9)(S20). The anchor lock-in schedule was not in any source we opened.

Subscription: this report was written on 25 September 2026, the day the issue opened. When we checked, trackers showed no category-wise data yet: total subscription was 0x, with QIB, NII and retail figures still awaited (S10). There is therefore no meaningful demand signal from the public book yet. Day-1 numbers are always partial, and QIB bids usually come in on the last day (S10).

GMP figures are unofficial, unregulated and conflicting: two trackers report Rs 113 and Rs 51.5 for the same day (S10)(S11)(S12). They say nothing about the business and play no part in this report's verdict.

DRHP - investor page

method: Primary sources: (1) the SEBI-hosted Abridged Prospectus summarising the RHP dated 21 Sep 2026 (S1), read in full, which gives restated FY24-FY26 and Q1 FY27 financials, KPIs, segment/geography/customer-concentration tables, objects, promoter holdings, top-10 risks and a litigation summary; (2) the full DRHP dated 10 Jul 2025 downloaded from the company's investor page (S3/S21), whose Our Business, Risk Factors, Objects of the Offer, Promoters/Group Companies, RPT summary and Outstanding Litigation sections were read page by page. The full RHP was not available as a readable document (the BSE/NSE copies returned 403 or timed out), so RHP-specific details not in the abridged prospectus come from secondary sources that summarise the RHP, and are cited to them. These include the capex line items and deployment schedule (S7), the Orient Electric name/trademark dispute (S8), FY26 capacity utilisation (S12) and June 2026 capacity (S6, S14). Where the DRHP and RHP differ (OFS cut from Rs 380 cr to Rs 232 cr, FY25 PAT Rs 532.91 mn vs Rs 533.21 mn, capex deployment moved later, CFO name), both are noted. Industry figures come from the company-commissioned 1Lattice report as reproduced in the prospectus. Several secondary pages carry no publication date, so the date recorded is the access date (25 Sep 2026). Some calculations are our own: FY26 growth, cumulative PAT vs operating cash flow, OFS share of the issue, and the approximate debt reduction. Gaps: anchor lock-in dates were not confirmed in any source opened; day-1 category-wise subscription figures had not been published when this was written; GMP figures conflict between trackers and are reported only as unofficial. Per the brief, all valuation metrics (P/E, EV/EBITDA, market-cap comparisons, peer multiples) were deliberately left out, even where sources gave them.
